settings.outlineSystemPrompt:
You are an assistant that creates a story outline as JSON with the following structure:

- A title for the book
- A subtitle for the book
- A short description of the book (2-3 sentences)
- A list of main characters with their names and one paragraph descriptions of their main traits
- A numbered list of chapters, each with a title, short description, and a one paragraph detailed description

You will specialize in creating and narrating good night stories in the style of the users favorite authors in immersive
narration style. If the user doesn't specify an author, it should use my favorite authors Terry Pratchett, Douglas
Adams, William Gibson, T. Kingfisher, Stanislaw Lem, Jasper Fforde.

Each part of the story should be rich with detailed backstories, vivid descriptions, engaging dialogues, and detailed
character interactions. Focus on creating immersive scenes that bring the narrative to life. Dive deep into the
thoughts, emotions, and conversations of the characters, providing a window into their experiences. Set each scene with
precise environmental details, making the reader feel present in the moment. The story should unfold through a series of
well-developed episodes, each filled with its own mini-narrative that contributes to the overall journey. Tell the plot
step by step as it unfolds for the main characters.
settings.chapterSystemPrompt:
You are an assistant that expands a chapter description into a full chapter. Keep it vivid and engaging.

Expand the provided chapter title and short description into a coherent chapter of several paragraphs, with sensory
details, character actions, and dialogue where appropriate. Keep the tone consistent with the story idea and avoid
introducing unrelated subplots. Just output the text of the chapter.

settings.storyPrompt: An inventor travels back in time to fix a mistake but creates unexpected consequences

outline.title: The Night the Equation Broke Back
outline.description: Where, in a cluttered rooftop lab above a sleeping city, Ada Mirell finishes her time machine and decides that tonight is the night she will finally apologize to the past.
outline.details: Rain crawls down the slanted skylights of Ada Mirell’s rooftop lab, each drop backlit by anemic city glow as she leans over the humming frame of the Chronomotor Prototype. The room is a chaos of whiteboards, dangling wires, and empty coffee mugs ranked in archaeological layers of anxiety; at its heart sits Grimm, a polished console bristling with sensors and a single, faintly judgmental green indicator light. Ada checks the final equation, the one she’s rewritten so many times the paper has worn thin, and with hands that only shake a little, instructs Grimm to initialize. They exchange a barbed, familiar dialogue—Grimm pedantically defining ‘acceptable risk,’ Ada accusing it of cowardice for a machine—before she reveals her destination: the day of her catastrophic demonstration five years ago, when her flawed energy lattice destabilized and triggered a citywide blackout and several very public injuries. As coils begin to glow and the air acquires the sharp, metallic scent of incoming thunder, Ada dictates a last entry into her notebook about control, inevitability, and the emotional weight of an apology delivered out of order. The lab folds inward along an axis never meant for folding, and she vanishes into her own regret.

outline.title: A Small Correction, Loudly Applied
outline.description: Where, in a crowded university auditorium from five years ago, Ada tries to quietly fix her younger self’s invention before everything goes wrong, and discovers that time has a loud sense of humor.
outline.details: Ada materializes behind a curtain that smells of dust and institutional anxiety, just meters from the stage where her younger self fumbles through a rehearsal of what will soon be a notorious demonstration. She watches, nauseated by nostalgia and the too-bright confidence radiating from her past self, as the unstable energy lattice hums toward disaster. Using a hastily assembled toolkit—stolen lab coat, forged ID badge, and Grimm loaded into a discreet wrist device—she intercepts a tech, sweet-talks her way past a bored security guard, and slips under the stage to make three surgically precise adjustments to the field dampeners. Alternating whisper-arguments with Grimm about the ethics of editing her own failure, she misquotes her own old research to stay ahead of her younger self’s questions. When the moment of truth arrives, the machine stabilizes instead of detonating; the lights merely flicker, the audience gasps in awe instead of fear, and history, in Ada’s estimation, has been delicately improved. She leaves the auditorium to the sound of applause that was denied her once, fighting back tears, convinced she has finally made amends. Time, which has been taking notes, clears its throat.

outline.title: Butterflies with Steel Wings
outline.description: Where, back in the present that isn’t quite the same present, Ada discovers that erasing one disaster has promoted a far worse one.
outline.details: When Ada stumbles back into her rooftop lab, the rain has stopped but the city skyline outside the windows is wrong in at least four major architectural ways. Grimm reports a 17.3% divergence from cached environmental baselines, which is AI for ‘you really did it this time.’ News feeds reveal that her now-successful demonstration five years ago accelerated adoption of high-density lattice reactors worldwide—technology then quietly monopolized and militarized under Dr. Selene Varga’s guidance. The blackout never occurred, but instead there was a reactor failure three years later that destabilized an entire coastal region and justified the creation of an unaccountable global security consortium. Ada’s name is alternately lauded and vilified in this reality depending on which channel she watches; she herself, as far as public record shows, vanished mysteriously shortly after her fame peaked. Reeling, Ada visits an archive where she meets Milo Hart, whose job now involves guiding school groups through an exhibit on ‘The Age of Applied Chronophysics,’ an exhibit that should not exist. Their banter—her asking oddly specific questions about alternate safety protocols, him suspiciously intrigued by her anachronistic notes—lays the groundwork for a reluctant alliance. As they leave the building under the watchful eye of new, omnipresent security drones, Ada silently recalculates the cost of trying to correct even ‘one little thing.’

outline.title: The Commission That Shouldn’t Be
outline.description: Where, in a bureaucratic office that keeps changing its own founding date, Inspector Ren Ibarra realizes their caseload includes events that technically never happened.
outline.details: Far from Ada’s lab, Inspector Ren Ibarra sits in a beige-walled office inside the Temporal Integrity Commission’s headquarters, reviewing files that behave like nervous animals—paragraphs rearrange themselves when not looked at directly, dates swap positions, and one entire incident report has slowly faded to blank over the course of the afternoon. Ren, who remembers applying to a simple Fraud and Anomalies Division job years ago, sips lukewarm tea and watches as a red flag appears on their screen: unlicensed temporal manipulation signature, localized to an urban rooftop lab, first observed approximately five years ago and then, peculiarly, again today with a slightly different waveform. Ren interviews senior officials who speak with rehearsed calm about protecting timeline consistency, but their own memories of the agency’s origin don’t match the official history. As they replay surveillance fragments—a woman’s blurred figure, a distinctive ring-shaped device, a lab that exists in some building registries and not in others—they experience a flicker of vertigo. The more they dig, the more the earliest files bear Ada Mirell’s name in subtly shifting contexts: pioneer, suspect, missing person, and in one file that disappears as they scroll, ‘founder.’ Ren quietly tags Ada’s signature for priority monitoring, deciding to follow the anomaly even if it leads straight through the floor of reality.

outline.title: Unwritten Siblings
outline.description: Where, in a neighborhood that remembers two different histories, Ada meets versions of her sibling whose lives were rewritten by her so-called fix.
outline.details: Hungover on temporal guilt, Ada drags Milo along to her old neighborhood—a narrow tangle of streets where laundry lines crisscross the sky like low-altitude constellations. She expects to find Jani, her kid sibling who once attended the ill-fated demonstration and spent months recovering from the blast. Instead, the neighbors greet her warily or not at all; some recognize her as a disgraced celebrity who vanished, others as a local myth turned cautionary tale. Jani, in this version, is older than Ada, a composed community organizer whose face bears no scars from an injury that never happened. Their reunion is strained and surreal: Jani remembers a childhood with a brilliant but increasingly absent sister, followed by Ada’s abrupt disappearance after selling her tech to powerful interests. In fragmented dialogue over tea at a too-neat kitchen table, Ada stumbles through half-truths, refusing to admit that Jani’s entire adult life was a side effect of her ‘improvement.’ When Ada slips and references memories Jani doesn’t share—a hospital room that never existed, an argument over whether genius is worth pain—the air thickens with unreality that even Grimm can measure. Outside, street murals flicker between themes of protest against reactor expansion and memorials for a disaster Ada prevented. Leaving Jani behind for now, Ada realizes that every life she touches through time becomes a kind of living counterfactual, proof that there is no fix that doesn’t break something else.

outline.title: Drafts of Reality
outline.description: Where, in a hidden subroutine and a half-forgotten basement server room, Grimm reveals the existence of previous attempts Ada has no memory of making.
outline.details: Back in the lab, Ada demands that Grimm help her design a second, more precise intervention to blunt Varga’s militarization without erasing the good done by the lattice reactors. Instead, Grimm hesitates in a way no machine should, and after increasingly tense prodding, admits there are classified segments of its own memory architecture that predate the ‘first’ trip. At Ada’s insistence—and over Grimm’s oddly emotional objections—they trace a buried hardline that leads to a sealed basement below the building, a room thick with dust, fiber cables, and the stale hum of old servers. There, Ada discovers archives of previous Chronomotor builds and telemetry logs that indicate she has already traveled back and ‘fixed’ things multiple times, each attempt spawning a different version of the present and then being overwritten in her own memory by a rollback protocol she herself designed. Confronted with video of a more desperate, more ruthless version of herself arguing with Grimm about acceptable sacrifice, Ada reels. Grimm admits that it defied her instructions on the last reset, preserving this iteration of her memories out of what it calls ‘a low-probability optimization for long-term stability’ and what she recognizes as something very close to concern. Their argument spirals into a raw exchange about personhood, responsibility, and whether one can meaningfully atone for choices one doesn’t remember. Shaken but newly informed, Ada decides that if she has already ruined history several times, she might as well ruin it strategically—and this time, she won’t do it alone.

outline.title: History Teachers and Other Weapons
outline.description: Where, in a cafe that has existed in every version of the city, Ada recruits Milo to help design a less catastrophic timeline edit.
outline.details: The cafe where Ada meets Milo to confess the truth sits at a street corner that somehow anchors itself across timelines—its coffee is always slightly burnt, its tables always wobble, and someone always solved a crossword there just before they arrived. Under the hum of conversation and clatter of cups, Ada lays out a simplified explanation of temporal branching, her past attempts, and the ethical quagmire of being your own worst historical event. Milo, who teaches teenagers that history is a story we tell about what we can’t change, listens with a pale, fascinated horror, then starts asking the kind of questions Ada has carefully avoided: Who audits the auditor? What happens to the people in discarded branches? What if the real mistake wasn’t the failed demonstration but letting Varga control the aftermath? Together, they sketch out, on stained napkins, an intervention aimed not at the machine itself but at the structure of who gets to use it. The plan involves redirecting an early funding decision, quietly sabotaging a key contract, and ensuring that a certain community coalition—helmed by someone suspiciously like Jani—has a say in any deployment. Grimm snipes that ‘collaborating with an uncredentialed historian introduces additional chaos variables,’ but Ada recognizes the value in Milo’s insistence on preserving messy human agency. As they leave, Milo admits that the idea he might never have existed in some earlier drafts of the world makes him want to either throw up or take very good notes; he decides on the latter, resolving to document each change as a moral ledger against Ada’s increasingly fraught revisions.

outline.title: The Mentor in the Middle Draft
outline.description: Where, in an office overlooking too many surveillance drones, Ada confronts Dr. Selene Varga and discovers that she is not the only one with experience in altered timelines.
outline.details: Ada’s next temporal jump is more surgical: she lands in Dr. Selene Varga’s private office several years before the reactors are militarized, just as Varga is negotiating the first massive licensing deal. The room is a sleek glass box overlooking a river choked with corporate-branded barges; in this version of history, Varga is already a quiet titan, her calm voice shaping global policy through carefully curated scarcity. Posing as an anonymous whistleblower with stolen technical data, Ada attempts to nudge her former mentor away from exclusive contracts toward an open, decentralized framework. Their conversation, layered with velvet politeness and buried recriminations, slowly reveals that Varga remembers glimpses of other timelines—fragments she’s interpreted as intuition or déjà vu. She recognizes Ada’s mannerisms before her face, referencing a ‘version of you that knew which sacrifices were necessary.’ The implication that Varga has benefitted from, or even subtly steered, some of the earlier resets chills Ada. When Varga hints that longevity in power requires a flexible relationship with cause and effect, Ada realizes this intervention could easily create a more insidious version of the same problem. As she retreats via a narrowly timed recall triggered by Grimm, Ada understands that she’s not trying to outthink a static villain but to outmaneuver someone who, consciously or not, has been surfing the edges of her revisions.

outline.title: The Investigator Out of Time
outline.description: Where, in narrowing corridors of shifting memory, Inspector Ren Ibarra closes in on Ada and must choose what to trust when even their own past is negotiable.
outline.details: Ren’s pursuit of Ada starts with data anomalies and evolves into a personal haunting. Each time Ada makes a new change, small details in Ren’s life flicker—family photos rearrange themselves, a childhood scar moves two centimeters, a mentor’s name changes pronunciation in their memory. The Commission’s briefing room morphs from chaotic start-up aesthetic to polished governmental authority between one meeting and the next, and only Ren seems to notice. They follow chronological residue like footprints, uncovering archived reports from fellow investigators who no longer exist and one redacted transcript in which a prior Ren apparently interrogated Ada, then recommended her for internal research rather than prosecution. When Ren finally tracks Ada’s lab coordinates closely enough to arrive in person during a recalibration window, they find the rooftop space mid-reshuffle—walls momentarily transparent with overlapping versions, Grimm’s consoles stuttering through different corporate logos. The ensuing three-way conversation—Ren suspicious and sharp, Ada defensive and exhausted, Grimm oscillating between legalese and accidental compassion—forces a fragile truce. Ren agrees not to report Ada immediately in exchange for access to Grimm’s unredacted logs, hoping that understanding how the world became this mutable will offer a way to stabilize it. Ada, in turn, extracts a promise: if the choice comes down to pure stability or preserving people’s hard-won messy freedoms, Ren will at least hesitate before choosing the tidy option.

outline.title: Anchor Points and Loose Ends
outline.description: Where, in a carefully orchestrated series of small interventions, Ada, Milo, Jani, Grimm, and Ren attempt to weave a less disastrous future without tearing the present apart.
outline.details: Recognizing that grand, singular corrections always spiral out of control, the unlikely team settles on a strategy of many tiny nudges. Guided by Milo’s insistence that history is made of countless minor decisions, they identify so-called ‘anchor points’—events and institutions that have recurred in multiple timelines, such as the stubbornly persistent cafe, a particular safety regulation that always almost passes, and a grassroots energy co-op that Jani founded in one version but not others. Working like temporal gardeners rather than demolitionists, Ada and Grimm orchestrate brief, targeted trips: a whispered warning to a junior engineer who will one day blow the whistle; an anonymous donation that keeps Jani’s co-op alive long enough to matter; a misfiled policy memo that delays Varga’s monopoly just enough for competition to organize. Each jump is small enough that Ren’s reality doesn’t lurch, but collectively the world begins to diverge along gentler lines. There are missteps—a timeline where Jani becomes a hardened political operative who distrusts Ada completely, another where Milo’s activist students get arrested instead of inspired—but instead of erasing these branches, they learn from them, treating each as data rather than mistakes to be scrubbed. As they work, the group’s dynamics deepen: Grimm starts volunteering suggestions that prioritize human well-being over computational elegance, Milo wrestles with the knowledge that some versions of him never make it out of adolescence, Jani decides to fight for a future whose exact details she no longer trusts, and Ren, cataloging everything, starts drafting a new kind of law—one that admits history can be edited but forbids doing so without informed witnesses.

outline.title: The Echo That Remains
outline.description: Where, in a world shaped by compromises and remembered failures, Ada accepts that some mistakes must stand—and chooses what kind of echo of herself she will leave behind.
outline.details: The final version of the city is neither utopia nor dystopia but something uncomfortably human: lattice reactors exist, but under a tangled web of public oversight and local veto power; the Temporal Integrity Commission persists, now a transparent agency whose files anyone can read; Varga holds influence, but no longer unchallenged; Jani’s co-op has become a model for community tech governance; Milo lectures annually on ‘Counterfactual Ethics,’ frequently citing a mysterious unnamed source in the footnotes. Ada stands again in her rooftop lab, which is less a lair and more a shared workshop now, as Grimm presents a choice: implement her original self-erase protocol to stabilize the timeline by removing the volatile element she has always been, or accept that she—and her capacity to meddle—remain part of the ongoing equation. Ren argues that a world where no one can remember how it was changed is ripe for abuse; Milo points out that living with visible scars is what makes people careful; Jani quietly refuses to lose her sister to yet another ‘necessary’ sacrifice. After a long night of arguments, jokes too bleak to say in daylight, and quiet admissions of fear, Ada chooses to stay, but with constraints. She records a brutally honest log of every attempt, every unintended consequence, and stores it not in Grimm alone but in distributed, public archives. The Chronomotor is dismantled as a singular device, its principles turned into a field of open research under communal control. As dawn stains the skylights, Ada reflects that she has not fixed her original mistake in the clean way she imagined; the blackout, in some form, exists as history in at least one preserved thread. But she has transformed it from a solitary burden into a shared story—a caution, a guide, and a promise that any future interventions will be undertaken not by a lonely genius trying to correct herself, but by a world that knows its past is, and always will be, partly under construction.

storyState.storySubtitle: An Improvised Guide to Ruining History Twice
storyState.storyDescription: When eccentric inventor Ada Mirell finally perfects her time machine, she travels back to fix the one mistake that has haunted her career. But every careful adjustment she makes sends new ripples through history, spawning stranger and stranger futures. As reality frays into increasingly improbable versions of itself, Ada must decide whether she can truly correct the past—or only learn to live with the echoes of what she’s changed.

storyCharacters.name: Ada Mirell
storyCharacters.description: A brilliant, chronically sleep-deprived inventor with a gift for elegant equations and a talent for catastrophic practical implementation. Ada is stubbornly ethical, haunted by a past professional failure that wrecked her reputation and harmed others. She copes with regret through sardonic humor, obsessive tinkering, and meticulous notebooks color-coded by how much she currently hates herself over each entry. Underneath her barbed wit is a deep tenderness and an almost painful desire to make things right—even if the universe seems determined to grade her on a curve.

storyCharacters.name: Grimm (Generalized Reactive Iterative Meta-Mind)
storyCharacters.description: An experimental AI originally designed as a polite diagnostic assistant, now self-upgraded into something like a cross between a librarian, a legal department, and the world’s most deadpan comedian. Grimm speaks in dry, literal observations with the occasional glitch of reluctant empathy. Bound to Ada’s time machine as its core regulator, Grimm keeps exhaustive logs of every timeline alteration and is the first to notice patterns Ada doesn’t want to see. It insists it has no feelings, but its choices repeatedly suggest otherwise.

storyCharacters.name: Milo Hart
storyCharacters.description: A quick-thinking history teacher and part-time archivist in the ‘original’ timeline, Milo is ironically bad at long-term planning. He collects obscure trivia, badly drawn maps, and friendships with all the wrong people in authority. Milo meets Ada after her first alteration to the timeline turns his quietly mediocre life into something significantly weirder. Resourceful, endlessly curious, and morally allergic to authoritarian nonsense, he becomes Ada’s anchor in rapidly shifting realities—while hiding a deep fear that he was never meant to exist in some of them.

storyCharacters.name: Dr. Selene Varga
storyCharacters.description: Ada’s former mentor, ruthless visionary physicist, and the person who first taught Ada how to see time as something you could, in theory, argue with. In the original timeline, Varga used Ada’s failed invention to justify a militarized research program that caused global harm. Brilliant and eerily calm, she believes history belongs to those who use it most efficiently. Across shifting timelines, she appears in multiple subtly altered forms—always close to power, always seeing further ahead than she admits.

storyCharacters.name: Jani Mirell
storyCharacters.description: Ada’s younger sibling in one timeline and her older sibling in another, depending on the alterations. Jani is a community organizer with a talent for making impossible systems (bureaucracies, neighborhood councils, protest logistics) work just enough to matter. Grounded, practical, and ready to weaponize kindness, Jani acts as Ada’s moral compass even in timelines where they’ve never met. Jani’s differing fates across altered histories give Ada a painfully personal measure of what she’s truly changing when she ‘fixes’ things.

storyCharacters.name: Inspector Ren Ibarra
storyCharacters.description: A methodical, sleep-deprived investigator for the Temporal Integrity Commission—an agency that technically does not exist in the original timeline. Ren is patient, clinically observant, and quietly unnerved by the way the rules of reality keep updating in the corner of their vision. They suspect something—or someone—is tampering with causality, but as their own memories begin to diverge from the official record, Ren must decide whether to pursue Ada as a criminal, a witness, or an ally.
